questions.question: Let \(A\) be an \(n \times n\) real matrix such that \(A^2 = I\) and \(y\) be an \(n\)-dimensional vector. Then the linear system of equations \(Ax = y\) has
options: more than one but finitely many independent solutions
questions.explanation: Given the linear system matrix equation \(A_{n \times n} X_{n \times n} = Y_{n \times 1}\) and the condition \(A^2 = I\). From the matrix property definition of powers: \[A^2 = I \implies AA = I\] By definition, if there exists a matrix \(B\) such that \(AB = BA = I\), then \(A\) is invertible and \(B = A^{-1}\). Here, the matrix \(A\) acts as its own inverse: \[\implies A \text{ is invertible, i.e., } A^{-1} \text{ exists and } A^{-1} = A\] \[\implies A \text{ is non-singular } (\text{det}(A) \neq 0)\] For any linear system of equations \(AX = Y\), if the coefficient matrix \(A\) is non-singular (or invertible), we can uniquely pre-multiply both sides by \(A^{-1}\): \[X = A^{-1}Y\] \[\therefore \text{A unique solution exists.}\] \[\boxed{\text{(B) a unique solution}}\]

questions.question: Let \(A = [a_{ij}], 1 \le i, j \le n\), with \(n \ge 3\) and \(a_{ij} = i.j\). Then the rank of \(A\) is
questions.explanation:
Given matrix \(A\) of order \(n \times n\): \[A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 & \cdots & n \\ 2 & 4 & 6 & \cdots & 2n \\ 3 & 6 & 9 & \cdots & 3n \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ n & 2n & 3n & \cdots & 3n \end{bmatrix}_{n \times n}\] Observing the rows, we can write them in terms of the first row \(R_1\): \[R_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 & \cdots & n \end{bmatrix}\] \[R_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 & 6 & \cdots & 2n \end{bmatrix} = 2R_1\] \[R_3 = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 6 & 9 & \cdots & 3n \end{bmatrix} = 3R_1\] \[\vdots\] \[R_n = \begin{bmatrix} n & 2n & 3n & \cdots & 3n \end{bmatrix} = nR_1\] We can perform elementary row operations to reduce the matrix to row echelon form: \[R_i \rightarrow R_i - iR_1 \quad \forall i = 2, 3, \dots, n\] \[A \sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 & \cdots & n \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \end{bmatrix}_{n \times n}\] \[\therefore \rho(A) = 1\] The rank is \(1\) because matrix \(A\) possesses only one linearly independent row. \[\boxed{\text{(B) 1}}\]
Key points
  • Linearly Dependent Rows: If all rows of a matrix can be expressed as scalar multiples of a single non-zero row (\(R_i = c_i R_1\)), the rank of that matrix is identically \(1\).

questions.question: The value of \(\int_{0}^{\infty} \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-x^2} e^{-y^2} \, dx \, dy\) is
questions.explanation:
The given double integral is: \[I = \int_{0}^{\infty} \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-x^2} e^{-y^2} \, dx \, dy\] Since the limits for both \(x\) and \(y\) are constants (independent of each other) and the integrand can be factored into a function of \(x\) and a function of \(y\), we can separate the double integral into the product of two independent single integrals: \[I = \left( \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-y^2} \, dy \right) \left( \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-x^2} \, dx \right)\] Let us evaluate the standard Gaussian integral \(J = \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-x^2} \, dx\) using the Gamma function substitution. Let \(x^2 = t \implies x = \sqrt{t} = t^{1/2}\). Differentiating both sides: \[dx = \frac{1}{2} t^{-1/2} \, dt\] The limits of integration remain unchanged: when \(x = 0\), \(t = 0\); and when \(x \to \infty\), \(t \to \infty\). Substitute these into the integral: \[J = \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-t} \cdot \frac{1}{2} t^{-1/2} \, dt\] \[J = \frac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{\infty} t^{\frac{1}{2} - 1} e^{-t} \, dt\] Using the definition of the Gamma function, \(\Gamma(n) = \int_{0}^{\infty} t^{n-1} e^{-t} \, dt\): \[J = \frac{1}{2} \Gamma\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\] Since \(\Gamma\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = \sqrt{\pi}\): \[J = \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-x^2} \, dx = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}\] Since the integral with respect to \(y\) has the identical form, its value is also: \[\int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-y^2} \, dy = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}\] Substituting these values back into the separated expression for \(I\): \[I = \left(\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}\right) = \frac{\pi}{4}\] \[\boxed{\text{(d) } \frac{\pi}{4}}\]
Key points
  • Separability Rule: \(\int_{a}^{b} \int_{c}^{d} f(x)g(y) \, dx \, dy = \left(\int_{a}^{b} f(x) \, dx\right) \left(\int_{c}^{d} g(y) \, dy\right)\).
  • Standard Gaussian Integral: \(\int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-x^2} \, dx = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}\).

questions.question: For real \(x\), the maximum value of \(\dfrac{e^{\sin x}}{e^{\cos x}}\) is
questions.explanation: The given function is: \[f(x) = \frac{e^{\sin x}}{e^{\cos x}} = e^{\sin x - \cos x}\] To find the maximum value, we need to maximize the exponent term \(g(x) = \sin x - \cos x\), since the exponential function \(e^u\) is monotonically increasing. Differentiating \(g(x)\) with respect to \(x\): \[g'(x) = \cos x - (-\sin x) = \cos x + \sin x\] Setting \(g'(x) = 0\) to find the stationary points: \[\cos x + \sin x = 0 \implies \tan x = -1\] \[x = \frac{3\pi}{4}, -\frac{\pi}{4}, \dots\] Now, we evaluate the second derivative to verify the local maximum condition: \[g''(x) = -\sin x + \cos x\] At \(x = \frac{3\pi}{4}\): \[\sin\left(\frac{3\pi}{4}\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \quad \cos\left(\frac{3\pi}{4}\right) = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\] \[g''\left(\frac{3\pi}{4}\right) = -\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) + \left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = -\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} = -\sqrt{2} < 0\] Since \(g''(x) < 0\), a local maximum occurs at \(x = \frac{3\pi}{4}\). The maximum value of \(g(x)\) is: \[g\left(\frac{3\pi}{4}\right) = \sin\left(\frac{3\pi}{4}\right) - \cos\left(\frac{3\pi}{4}\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - \left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = \frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2}\] Substituting this value back into the original function \(f(x)\): \[f_{\max} = e^{\sqrt{2}}\] \[\boxed{\text{(c) } e^{\sqrt{2}}}\]

questions.question: Consider the function \(f(x) = |x|^3\), where \(x\) is real. Then the function \(f(x)\) at \(x = 0\) is
questions.explanation: The given function is defined as: \[f(x) = |x|^3 = \begin{cases} x^3, & \text{if } x > 0 \\ -x^3, & \text{if } x < 0 \\ 0, & \text{if } x = 0 \end{cases}\] Let us evaluate the continuity and subsequent higher-order derivatives at the origin: Checking the limit from both directions: \[\lim_{x \to 0^+} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 0^-} f(x) = f(0) = 0\] The function is continuous at \(x = 0\). Differentiating the piecewise components for non-zero points: \[f'(x) = \begin{cases} 3x^2, & \text{if } x > 0 \\ -3x^2, & \text{if } x < 0 \end{cases}\] Evaluating the left-hand derivative and right-hand derivative at the boundary: \[\text{LHD} = \lim_{x \to 0^-} (-3x^2) = 0\] \[\text{RHD} = \lim_{x \to 0^+} (3x^2) = 0\] Since the directional derivatives match, the first derivative exists at \(x = 0\) with a value of \(0\). \[f'(x) = \begin{cases} 3x^2, & \text{if } x > 0 \\ -3x^2, & \text{if } x < 0 \\ 0, & \text{if } x = 0 \end{cases}\] Differentiating the first derivative function for non-zero points: \[f''(x) = \begin{cases} 6x, & \text{if } x > 0 \\ -6x, & \text{if } x < 0 \end{cases}\] Evaluating the limits from both sides at \(x = 0\): \[\lim_{x \to 0^-} f''(x) = \lim_{x \to 0^-} (-6x) = 0\] \[\lim_{x \to 0^+} f''(x) = \lim_{x \to 0^+} (6x) = 0\] Since both directional limits are equal, the second derivative exists at \(x = 0\) with a value of \(0\). \[f''(x) = \begin{cases} 6x, & \text{if } x > 0 \\ -6x, & \text{if } x < 0 \\ 0, & \text{if } x = 0 \end{cases}\] Differentiating the second derivative function for non-zero points: \[f'''(x) = \begin{cases} 6, & \text{if } x > 0 \\ -6, & \text{if } x < 0 \end{cases}\] Evaluating the behavior at the boundary point: \[\lim_{x \to 0^-} f'''(x) = -6\] \[\lim_{x \to 0^+} f'''(x) = 6\] Because the left-hand limit and right-hand limit are unequal, the third derivative fails to exist at \(x = 0\). Consequently, the function is differentiable exactly twice at the origin. \[\boxed{\text{(c) Twice differentiable but not thrice}}\]

questions.question: The boundary-value problem \(y''+\lambda y=0,\ y(0)=y(\pi)=0\) will have non-zero solutions if and only if the values of \(\lambda\) are
questions.explanation:
Given the boundary value problem \[y'' + \lambda y = 0,\ \text{with boundary conditions}\ \ y(0) = 0,\ y(\pi) = 0\] We need to determine the values of \(\lambda\) for which non-zero solutions exist.
Method 1 (Characteristic Equation Method)
Assume a solution of the form \(y = e^{mx}\) Substituting into the differential equation, \[m^2 + \lambda = 0\] For non-trivial solutions, we analyze the possible values of \(\lambda\). Case 1: \(\lambda=0\)
The differential equation becomes \[y'' = 0\] Integrating twice, \[y = C_1 + C_2x\] Applying \(y(0) = 0,\ C_1 = 0\) and \(y(\pi) = 0.\ C_2 = 0.\) Only the trivial solution exists. Case 2: \(\lambda<0\)
Let \(\lambda = -\mu^2,\ \mu > 0.\) \[y'' - \mu^2y = 0\] The general solution is \[y = C_1e^{\mu x} + C_2e^{-\mu x}\] Applying the boundary conditions leads only to \(C_1 = C_2 = 0.\) Hence no non-zero solution exists. Case 3: \(\lambda>0\)
Let \(\lambda = \alpha^2.\) The roots are \(m = \pm i\alpha.\) Therefore, \[y = C_1\cos(\alpha x) + C_2\sin(\alpha x)\] Using \(y(0) = 0,\ C_1 = 0.\) Applying \(y(\pi) = 0,\) we obtain \[C_2\sin(\alpha\pi) = 0\] For a non-zero solution, \(C_2\neq 0,\) therefore \[\sin(\alpha\pi) = 0\] Thus, \[\alpha = n, \qquad n = 1,2,3,\ldots\] and hence \(\lambda=n^2.\) Therefore, \[\lambda=1,4,9,\ldots\]
Method 2 (Eigenvalue Interpretation)
The problem is a standard Sturm--Liouville eigenvalue problem. For boundary conditions of the form \(y(0) = 0,\ y(L) = 0,\) the eigenvalues are \[\lambda_n = \left(\frac{n\pi}{L}\right)^2, \qquad n = 1,2,3,\ldots\] Here, \(L = \pi.\) Therefore, \[\lambda_n = \left(\frac{n\pi}{\pi}\right)^2 = n^2\] Hence, \[\lambda = 1,4,9,\ldots\]
\[\boxed{\text{(C)}\ 1,4,9,\ldots}\]
Key points
  • A boundary value problem admits a non-trivial solution only for specific values of the parameter \(\lambda\), called eigenvalues.
  • For \(\lambda>0\), the solutions are sinusoidal and can satisfy both boundary conditions simultaneously.
  • For \(\lambda\le 0\), only the trivial solution satisfies the given boundary conditions.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not include \(n=0\); it corresponds to the trivial solution.

questions.question: Identify the Newton-Raphson iteration scheme for finding the square root of \(2\)
questions.explanation:
We want to find the square root of 2 using the Newton-Raphson method. This can be modeled as finding the root of the equation: \[x = \sqrt{2} \implies x^2 = 2 \implies f(x) = x^2 - 2 = 0\] Take the first derivative of \(f(x)\) with respect to \(x\): \[f'(x) = 2x\] Substitute \(f(x)\) and \(f'(x)\) into the standard Newton-Raphson iteration formula: \[x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}\] \[x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{x_n^2 - 2}{2x_n}\] Combine the terms over a common denominator: \[\begin{aligned} x_{n+1} &= \dfrac{x_n(2x_n) - \left(x_n^2 - 2\right)}{2x_n} \\[1.5ex] &= \dfrac{2x_n^2 - x_n^2 + 2}{2x_n} \\[1.5ex] &= \dfrac{x_n^2 + 2}{2x_n} \\[1.5ex] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \left( x_n + \dfrac{2}{x_n} \right) \end{aligned}\] This derived iteration scheme matches Option A. \[\boxed{\text{A. } x_{n+1} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(x_n + \dfrac{2}{x_n}\right)}\]
Key points
  • Babylonian Square Root Method: The Newton-Raphson formulation for square roots simplifies to the ancient Babylonian averaging method, which iteratively computes the arithmetic mean of the current guess \(x_n\) and \(\frac{N}{x_n}\).

questions.question: Let \(x(t)\) be a continuous-time, real-valued signal band-limited to \(F\) Hz. The Nyquist sampling rate (in Hz) for\[y(t)=x(0.5t)+x(t)-x(2t)\]is
questions.explanation:
Theory: According to the time-scaling property of the Continuous-Time Fourier Transform (CTFT), if \(x(t) \xleftrightarrow{\mathcal{F}} X(f)\), then: \[x(at) \xleftrightarrow{\mathcal{F}} \frac{1}{|a|} X\left(\frac{f}{a}\right)\] Time compression (\(|a| > 1\)) expands the frequency spectrum by a factor of \(|a|\), whereas time expansion (\(|a| < 1\)) compresses the spectrum. The Nyquist sampling rate is defined as \(f_s = 2 f_{\max}\). Given that \(x(t)\) is band-limited to \(F\text{ Hz}\), its highest frequency component is \(f_{\max} = F\text{ Hz}\). Analyzing each term in \(y(t) = x(0.5t) + x(t) - x(2t)\):
  • For \(x(0.5t)\), \(a = 0.5 < 1\) (time expansion), so its highest frequency component is \(0.5F\text{ Hz}\).
  • For \(x(t)\), \(a = 1\), so its highest frequency component remains \(F\text{ Hz}\).
  • For \(x(2t)\), \(a = 2 > 1\) (time compression), so its highest frequency component becomes \(2F\text{ Hz}\).
The maximum frequency component \(f_{\max, y}\) present in the composite signal \(y(t)\) is the maximum among all terms: \[f_{\max, y} = \max(0.5F, \, F, \, 2F) = 2F \text{ Hz}.\] Therefore, the Nyquist sampling rate \(f_s\) is: \[f_s = 2 \times f_{\max, y} = 2(2F) = 4F.\] Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\text{(C) }4F}\]
Key points
  • Time-scaling parameter \(a\) scales the frequency range by \(|a|\).
  • For a linear combination of signals, the maximum frequency of the sum is the maximum of the individual signals' maximum frequencies.
  • The Nyquist sampling rate is twice the highest frequency present in the signal (\(f_s = 2 f_{\max}\)).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse time compression with frequency compression; compressing in time expands the frequency bandwidth.
  • Do not add the bandwidths of individual terms when taking a sum or difference of signals.
  • Do not forget to multiply the maximum frequency \(f_{\max, y}\) by \(2\) to calculate the Nyquist rate.

questions.question: Let the signal \(x(t)\) have the Fourier transform \(X(\omega)\). Consider the signal\[y(t)=\frac{d}{dt}\left[x(t-t_d)\right],\]where \(t_d\) is an arbitrary delay. The magnitude of the Fourier transform of \(y(t)\) is given by
questions.explanation:
Theory: Time delay introduces a phase shift, while differentiation multiplies the spectrum by \(j\omega\). Given,\[x(t) \xleftrightarrow{\mathcal{F}} X(\omega).\]Using the time-delay property,\[x(t-t_d) \xleftrightarrow{\mathcal{F}} e^{-j\omega t_d}X(\omega).\]Applying the differentiation property,\[\frac{d}{dt}x(t-t_d) \xleftrightarrow{\mathcal{F}} j\omega\,e^{-j\omega t_d}X(\omega).\]Taking magnitude,\[|Y(\omega)| = |j\omega| \,|e^{-j\omega t_d}| \,|X(\omega)|.\]Since\[|j|=1, \qquad |e^{-j\omega t_d}|=1,\]we obtain\[|Y(\omega)| = |\omega|\,|X(\omega)|.\]Hence,\[\boxed{\text{(A) }|\omega|\,|X(\omega)|}\]
Key points
  • Differentiation multiplies the spectrum by \(j\omega\).
  • Time delay contributes only a phase factor of unit magnitude.
  • The magnitude of \(e^{-j\omega t_d}\) is always \(1\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not include the delay term while computing magnitude.
  • Use \(|\omega|\), not \(\omega\), for the magnitude expression.
  • Remember that \(|j|=1\).

Let \(V_1 = V_2 = 0\) and \(R_1 = 20\text{ k}\Omega\). Assume that the op-amp is ideal except for a non-zero input bias current. What is the value of \(R_2\) for the output voltage of the op-amp to be zero?
questions.explanation:
To make the output voltage zero, the voltage drops produced by the input bias currents at both input terminals must be equal. For minimum output offset, \[R_2=R_{\text{eq}}\] where \(R_{\text{eq}}\) is the equivalent resistance seen by the inverting terminal. Since \(V_1=V_2=0\), \[R_{\text{eq}} = 20\,\text{k}\Omega \parallel 20\,\text{k}\Omega \parallel 100\,\text{k}\Omega\] \[R_{\text{eq}} = \frac{20\times20}{20+20} \parallel 100 = 10\,\text{k}\Omega \parallel 100\,\text{k}\Omega\] \[R_2 = \frac{10\times100}{10+100} = 9.09\,\text{k}\Omega \approx 9.1\,\text{k}\Omega\] Therefore, \[R_2=9.1\,\text{k}\Omega\] \[\boxed{\text{(b) }9.1\,\text{k}\Omega}\]
Key points
  • To compensate the effect of input bias current, make the equivalent resistance seen by both input terminals equal.
  • The equivalent resistance at the inverting input is obtained by replacing all voltage sources with their internal resistance (ideal voltage sources become shorts).

questions.explanation: \[V_{+}=0 \;\Rightarrow\; V_{-}=0\] Hence, the voltage at port 1 of the feedback network is \[V_1=0\] Since the op-amp input draws zero current, \[I_1=\frac{V_i-0}{1\,\text{k}\Omega} =\frac{V_i}{1\,\text{k}\Omega}\] The given \(Z\)-parameters are \[Z_{11}=Z_{22}=11\,\text{k}\Omega,\qquad Z_{12}=Z_{21}=1\,\text{k}\Omega\] Using the \(Z\)-parameter equations, \[V_1=Z_{11}I_1+Z_{12}I_2\] \[0=11\,\text{k}\Omega\,I_1+1\,\text{k}\Omega\,I_2\] \[I_2=-11I_1\] Now, \[V_o=V_2=Z_{21}I_1+Z_{22}I_2\] \[V_o =1\,\text{k}\Omega\,I_1 +11\,\text{k}\Omega(-11I_1) =-120\,\text{k}\Omega\,I_1\] Substituting \(I_1=\dfrac{V_i}{1\,\text{k}\Omega}\), \[V_o =-120\,\text{k}\Omega \left(\frac{V_i}{1\,\text{k}\Omega}\right) =-120V_i\] Therefore, \[A_v=\frac{V_o}{V_i}=-120\] \[\boxed{\text{(d) }-120}\]

questions.question: Consider the triangular wave generator shown below. Assume that the op-amps are ideal and have \(\pm 12\text{ V}\) power supply. If the input is a \(\pm 5\text{ V}\) \(50\text{ Hz}\) square wave of duty cycle \(50\%\), the condition that results in a triangular wave of peak to peak amplitude \(5\text{ V}\) and frequency \(50\text{ Hz}\) at the output is
questions.explanation: The first op-amp is an integrator and the second op-amp is an inverting amplifier. For the integrator, \[\left|\frac{dV}{dt}\right| =\frac{V_{in}}{R_iC} =\frac{5}{10C} =\frac{0.5}{C}\;\text{V/ms}\] where \(R_i=10\,\text{k}\Omega\) and \(C\) is in \(\mu\text{F}\). The input is a \(50\,\text{Hz}\) square wave, hence \[T=\frac{1}{50}=20\,\text{ms}, \qquad \frac{T}{2}=10\,\text{ms}\] During one half-cycle, the integrator output changes by \[\Delta V =\frac{0.5}{C}\times10 =\frac{5}{C}\;\text{V}\] The second stage is an inverting amplifier with gain \[A_v=-\frac{R}{1} =-R\] since the input resistor is \(1\,\text{k}\Omega\) and the feedback resistor is \(R\,\text{k}\Omega\). Therefore, the output peak-to-peak voltage is \[V_{o(pp)} = R\left(\frac{5}{C}\right)\] Given, \[V_{o(pp)}=5\,\text{V}\] Hence, \[R\left(\frac{5}{C}\right)=5\] \[\boxed{\text{(b) }\dfrac{R}{C}=1}\]

questions.explanation: Consider the two operating conditions of the switch. Case 1: \(V_{in}>0\) The switch is closed. The first op-amp is an inverting amplifier with unity gain, hence \[V_1=-V_{in}\] Applying KCL at the inverting input of the second op-amp, \[V_o = -\left( \frac{R}{R}V_{in} + \frac{R}{0.5R}V_1 \right)\] \[V_o = -\left( V_{in}+2(-V_{in}) \right) = V_{in}\] Case 2: \(V_{in}<0\) The switch is open, so only the upper input is active. \[V_o = -\frac{R}{R}V_{in} = -V_{in}\] Thus, \[V_o= \begin{cases} V_{in}, & V_{in}>0\\ -V_{in}, & V_{in}<0 \end{cases} = |V_{in}|\] Hence, the circuit produces the absolute value of the input, i.e., it is a precision full-wave rectifier. \[\boxed{\text{(d) Precision rectifier}}\]

questions.question: The input signal shown in the figure shown above is fed to a Schmitt trigger. The signal has a square wave amplitude of \(6\text{ V}\) p-p. It is corrupted by an additive high frequency noise of amplitude \(8\text{ V}\) p-p. Which one of the following is an appropriate choice for the upper and lower trip points of the Schmitt trigger to recover a square wave of the same frequency from the corrupted input signal \(V_{\text{i}}\) ?
questions.explanation:
The input is a square wave of amplitude \(6\,\text{V}_{\text{p-p}}\), i.e., \[V_{i}=\pm 3\,\text{V}.\] The additive noise has an amplitude of \(8\,\text{V}_{\text{p-p}}\), i.e., \[V_{\text{noise}}=\pm 4\,\text{V}.\] Hence, the noisy input varies as: \[\text{Positive level: }+3\pm4 \Rightarrow -1\,\text{V}\ \text{to}\ +7\,\text{V},\] \[\text{Negative level: }-3\pm4 \Rightarrow -7\,\text{V}\ \text{to}\ +1\,\text{V}.\] To recover the original square wave, the Schmitt trigger thresholds must satisfy:
  • Upper trip point \(<+3\,\text{V}\) so that the positive level always crosses it.
  • Upper trip point \(>+1\,\text{V}\) so that noise during the negative level cannot cause false triggering.
  • Lower trip point \(>-3\,\text{V}\) so that the negative level always crosses it.
  • Lower trip point \(<-1\,\text{V}\) so that noise during the positive level cannot cause false triggering.
Among the given options, only \[\boxed{\pm2.0\,\text{V}}\] satisfies all these conditions. \[\boxed{\text{(b) Upper and lower trip points }=\pm2.0\,\text{V}}\]
Key points
  • Noise amplitude is half of the peak-to-peak value.
  • Schmitt trigger thresholds must lie between the noise-affected voltage ranges.
  • Proper hysteresis prevents false triggering due to high-frequency noise.

questions.question: When light falls on the photodiode shown in the following circuit, the reverse saturation current of the photodiode changes from \(100~\mu\text{A}\) to \(200~\mu\text{A}\). Assuming the op-amp to be ideal, the output voltage, \(V_{out}\), of the circuit
questions.explanation: The circuit is a transimpedance amplifier. Since the non-inverting terminal is grounded, \[V_{-}=V_{+}=0\,\text{V}.\] The photocurrent flows through the feedback resistor, so \[V_{out}=-I_{ph}R_f.\] Initially, \[I_{ph}=100\,\mu\text{A}, \qquad R_f=10\,\text{k}\Omega.\] Hence, \[V_{out}=-(100\times10^{-6})(10\times10^3) =-1\,\text{V}.\] When light increases, \[I_{ph}=200\,\mu\text{A},\] therefore, \[V_{out}=-(200\times10^{-6})(10\times10^3) =-2\,\text{V}.\] Thus, the output changes from \[-1\,\text{V}\rightarrow -2\,\text{V}.\] \[\boxed{\text{(d) Changes from }-1\,\text{V}\text{ to }-2\,\text{V}}\]

questions.question: A logic circuit implements the Boolean function \(f = \bar x.y + x. \bar y. \bar z\) . It is found that the input combination \(x=y=1\) can never occur. Taking this into account, a simplified expression for \(f\) is given by
questions.explanation:
The function is \[f = \bar x.y + x. \bar y. \bar z\] Expanding to obtain canonical SOP form: \[f= \bar x.y. (z + \bar z) + x. \bar y. \bar z = \bar x.y.z + \bar x. y. \bar z +x. \bar y. \bar z\] The minterm indices are: \[f = \Sigma m (2,3,4)\] It is also mentioned that the input combination \(x=y=1\) can never occur. Thus minterms \(110\) and \(111\) are invalid and must be considered as don't-cares. Thus the final minterms are: \[f = \Sigma m (2,3,4) + \Sigma d(6,7)\] The K-Map is drawn as: The final minimal SOP expression is \(f = x \bar z + y\) \[\boxed{(D)\; y+x .\bar z}\]

  • Canonical SOP (also called Sum of Minterms) is the complete, unsimplified representation where every term contains all input variables of the function, either in complemented or uncomplemented form.

questions.explanation: From figure, Pulse width = \(T\) Time period of clock pulse = \(T_C\) From given figure, \(T = 6T_C\) , but during this \(6T_C\) duration, number of active edges of clocks = 7. questions.question:
8-bit signed integers in 2’s complement form are read into the accumulator of an 8085 microprocessor from an input/output port using the following assembly language program segment with symbolic addresses.
LabelMnemonics
BEGIN :IN PORT
RAL
JNC BEGIN
RET
RAR
END :HLT
This program:
options: halts upon reading a negative number
halts upon reading a positive number
questions.explanation:
The execution of the program proceeds as follows:
InstructionOperation
IN PORT\(A \leftarrow \text{PORT}\)
RALCase 1: Let the number be positive, i.e., \(00000110\). After RAL, the MSB of the accumulator rotates into carry: \(\text{Carry} = 0\). Since JNC is true, the same process repeats (loop continues).
Case 2: If the number is negative, i.e., \(10000001\). After RAL, the MSB rotates into carry: \(\text{Carry} = 1\). Since JNC is no longer true, the microprocessor exits the loop.
Thus, the program continuously reads input from the port and rotates the accumulator left, checking the carry (which reflects the MSB/sign bit) after each rotation. The loop continues as long as the input is non-negative (MSB \(= 0\)), and halts as soon as a negative number (MSB \(= 1\)) is read. \[\boxed{(A)\quad \text{The program halts upon reading a negative number}}\]
Key points
  • The RAL (Rotate Accumulator Left) instruction shifts all bits left by one position, with the MSB moving into the Carry flag and the previous Carry moving into the LSB.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse RAL (which rotates the MSB into Carry and Carry into LSB --- a 9-bit rotation including Carry) with RLC (which rotates the MSB into both Carry and LSB directly, an 8-bit rotation); the carry flag behavior differs subtly between the two.
  • Do not assume the loop continues indefinitely; the Carry flag directly mirrors the sign bit only on the first RAL after IN PORT, so the test must occur immediately after rotation.
  • Remember that JNC jumps (continues the loop) when Carry \(=0\), and falls through (exits the loop) when Carry \(=1\) --- the loop exit condition is the negative number case, not the positive one.

questions.question: A feedback control system with high gain \(K\), is shown in the figure below: Then the closed loop transfer function is
options: sensitive to perturbations in \(G(s)\) but not to perturbations in \(H(s)\)
sensitive to perturbations in \(H(s)\) but not to perturbations in \(G(s)\)
questions.explanation:
The closed-loop transfer function of the given control system is: \[T(s) = \frac{K G(s)}{1 + K G(s) H(s)}\] Sensitivity with respect to forward path \(G(s)\):
\[S_{G}^{T} = \frac{\partial T}{\partial G} \cdot \frac{G}{T}\] Differentiating \(T(s)\) with respect to \(G(s)\): \[\frac{\partial T}{\partial G} = \frac{[1 + K G(s) H(s)]K - K G(s)[K H(s)]}{[1 + K G(s) H(s)]^2}\] \[S_{G}^{T} = \frac{G}{T} \times \frac{K}{[1 + K G(s) H(s)]^2} = \frac{1}{1 + K G(s) H(s)}\] Given that the forward path gain \(K\) is very high (\(K \to \infty\)): \[S_{G}^{T} \to 0 \quad \text{(System becomes less sensitive to } G(s)\text{)}\] Sensitivity with respect to feedback path \(H(s)\):
\[S_{H}^{T} = \frac{\partial T}{\partial H} \cdot \frac{H}{T}\] Differentiating \(T(s)\) with respect to \(H(s)\): \[\frac{\partial T}{\partial H} = \frac{-[K G(s)] \cdot [K G(s)]}{[1 + K G(s) H(s)]^2}\] \[S_{H}^{T} = -\frac{K G(s)}{[1 + K G(s) H(s)]^2} \cdot \frac{[1 + K G(s) H(s)] H(s)}{K G(s)}\] \[S_{H}^{T} = -\frac{K G(s) H(s)}{1 + K G(s) H(s)}\] As the forward path gain \(K \to \infty\): \[S_{H}^{T} \to -1 \implies |S_{H}^{T}| \to 1 \quad \text{(Highly sensitive to } H(s)\text{)}\] \[\boxed{\text{(C) sensitive to perturbations in $H(s)$ but not to perturbations in $G(s)$}}\]
Key points
  • Sensitivity function \(S_{X}^{T} = \dfrac{\% \text{ change in } T}{\% \text{ change in } X} = \dfrac{\partial T}{\partial X} \cdot \dfrac{X}{T}\).
  • Increasing the loop gain decreases the system sensitivity to variations in the forward path elements but increases dependency on the accuracy of feedback path elements.

Common data for Q5.07.1 and Q5.07.2 A transfer function with unity DC gain has three poles at -1, -2, and -3 and no finite zeros. A plant with this transfer function is connected with a proportional controller of gain \(K\) in the forward path, in a unity feedback configuration.

The transfer function is
questions.explanation: Given the plant transfer function has three poles at \(-1\), \(-2\), and \(-3\) with no finite zeros, it can be represented as: \[G(s) = \frac{k}{(s+1)(s+2)(s+3)}\] For unity DC gain, we substitute \(s = 0\): \[G(0) = \frac{k}{(0+1)(0+2)(0+3)} = 1 \implies k = 6\] Thus, the plant transfer function is: \[\boxed{(B) \ \ G(s) = \frac{6}{(s+1)(s+2)(s+3)}}\]

The open-loop transfer function is, \[G(s)=\frac{K_ce^{-s}}{s+1}\] \[\angle G(j\omega) =-\omega-\tan^{-1}\omega\] At the phase crossover frequency, \[\angle G(j\omega_{pc})=-180^\circ=-\pi\] \[\omega+\tan^{-1}\omega=\pi\] Solving the above equation by trail of options, we find \(\omega=2.03~\text{rad/s}\) satisfies the above equation. \[\boxed{(D)\;2.03}\]
Key points
  • A transport delay \(e^{-sT}\) contributes a phase lag of \(-\omega T\;\text{radians}.\)
  • We can also solve the equation by using \(\tan^{-1}\omega\) \(\approx\) \(\omega-\dfrac{\omega^3}{3}\) \(+\) .....
